units.title: Thyroid physiology → Hypothyroidism
units.guide: Pregnancy alters thyroid binding and total hormone measurements while preserving a euthyroid free-hormone state. Learn fetal dependence on maternal thyroxine early in gestation, then distinguish hypothyroid replacement from trimester-specific antithyroid therapy. Focus for this checkpoint: Thyroid physiology, Fetal thyroid, Hypothyroidism.

units.title: Hyperthyroidism & Thyroid storm
units.guide: Pregnancy alters thyroid binding and total hormone measurements while preserving a euthyroid free-hormone state. Learn fetal dependence on maternal thyroxine early in gestation, then distinguish hypothyroid replacement from trimester-specific antithyroid therapy. Focus for this checkpoint: Hyperthyroidism, Thyroid storm.

units.title: Diabetes physiology & Placental transfer
units.guide: As placental hormones rise, pregnancy becomes progressively insulin resistant. Separate pregestational diabetes from gestational diabetes by timing, congenital-malformation risk, resolution after birth, and treatment class. Focus for this checkpoint: Diabetes physiology, Placental transfer.

units.title: Diabetes classification → GDM timing
units.guide: As placental hormones rise, pregnancy becomes progressively insulin resistant. Separate pregestational diabetes from gestational diabetes by timing, congenital-malformation risk, resolution after birth, and treatment class. Focus for this checkpoint: Diabetes classification, White classification, GDM timing.

units.title: GDM follow-up → Diabetes management
units.guide: As placental hormones rise, pregnancy becomes progressively insulin resistant. Separate pregestational diabetes from gestational diabetes by timing, congenital-malformation risk, resolution after birth, and treatment class. Focus for this checkpoint: GDM follow-up, Diabetes imaging, Diabetes management.

units.title: Pregestational diabetes & HbA1c and anomalies
units.guide: Pregestational diabetes is identified by overt glycemic thresholds and requires early anomaly-focused assessment. Master the HbA1c risk bands, key cardiac associations, and prevention before conception. Focus for this checkpoint: Pregestational diabetes, HbA1c and anomalies.

units.title: Diabetes imaging → Preconception prevention
units.guide: Pregestational diabetes is identified by overt glycemic thresholds and requires early anomaly-focused assessment. Master the HbA1c risk bands, key cardiac associations, and prevention before conception. Focus for this checkpoint: Diabetes imaging, Congenital anomalies, Preconception prevention.

units.title: Pre-GDM complications & Antenatal surveillance
units.guide: A pregestational-diabetes pregnancy needs structured antenatal, eye, urinary, fetal, and Doppler surveillance. Link each test to its purpose, then apply the delivery plan and preventive measures. Focus for this checkpoint: Pre-GDM complications, Antenatal surveillance.

units.title: Diabetes imaging → Pre-GDM treatment
units.guide: A pregestational-diabetes pregnancy needs structured antenatal, eye, urinary, fetal, and Doppler surveillance. Link each test to its purpose, then apply the delivery plan and preventive measures. Focus for this checkpoint: Diabetes imaging, Antenatal surveillance, Fetal surveillance, Doppler, Pre-GDM treatment.

units.title: Delivery timing & Delivery planning
units.guide: A pregestational-diabetes pregnancy needs structured antenatal, eye, urinary, fetal, and Doppler surveillance. Link each test to its purpose, then apply the delivery plan and preventive measures. Focus for this checkpoint: Delivery timing, Delivery planning.

units.title: GDM features → DIPSI procedure
units.guide: Use the nonfasting DIPSI screening pathway at the right visit and interpret 2-hour values correctly. Then connect glucose strata to nutrition, insulin, follow-up frequency, and Government of India treatment guidance. Focus for this checkpoint: GDM features, GDM investigations, DIPSI screening, DIPSI procedure.

units.title: DIPSI procedure → GDM management
units.guide: Use the nonfasting DIPSI screening pathway at the right visit and interpret 2-hour values correctly. Then connect glucose strata to nutrition, insulin, follow-up frequency, and Government of India treatment guidance. Focus for this checkpoint: DIPSI procedure, DIPSI interpretation, GDM management.

units.title: GDM targets → GDM follow-up → GOI GDM guidance
units.guide: Use the nonfasting DIPSI screening pathway at the right visit and interpret 2-hour values correctly. Then connect glucose strata to nutrition, insulin, follow-up frequency, and Government of India treatment guidance. Focus for this checkpoint: GDM targets, GDM management, GDM follow-up. It also includes GOI GDM guidance.

units.title: Medical nutrition therapy & Metformin
units.guide: Diet is structured, not restrictive: balance macronutrients, spread intake through the day, and adjust calories to BMI. Know where metformin and glyburide fit, including practical dose ceilings and adverse effects. Focus for this checkpoint: Medical nutrition therapy, Metformin.

units.title: Metformin & Glyburide
units.guide: Diet is structured, not restrictive: balance macronutrients, spread intake through the day, and adjust calories to BMI. Know where metformin and glyburide fit, including practical dose ceilings and adverse effects. Focus for this checkpoint: Metformin, Glyburide.

units.title: Insulin basics → Insulin dosing
units.guide: Insulin is the core therapy when glucose targets require it. Learn the premix formulation, dose-adjustment algorithm, delivery thresholds, labor fluid-insulin table, and the different postnatal plans for GDM versus pre-GDM. Focus for this checkpoint: Insulin basics, Insulin requirements, Insulin administration, Insulin dosing.

units.title: Insulin titration → Intrapartum diabetes
units.guide: Insulin is the core therapy when glucose targets require it. Learn the premix formulation, dose-adjustment algorithm, delivery thresholds, labor fluid-insulin table, and the different postnatal plans for GDM versus pre-GDM. Focus for this checkpoint: Insulin titration, Delivery timing, Intrapartum diabetes.

units.title: Intrapartum diabetes → Postpartum pre-GDM
units.guide: Insulin is the core therapy when glucose targets require it. Learn the premix formulation, dose-adjustment algorithm, delivery thresholds, labor fluid-insulin table, and the different postnatal plans for GDM versus pre-GDM. Focus for this checkpoint: Intrapartum diabetes, Postpartum GDM, Postpartum pre-GDM.

units.title: Maternal diabetes complications & Hypoglycemia
units.guide: Trace maternal hyperglycemia through infection, fluid, placental, and eye complications, then map the fetal and neonatal effects of fetal hyperinsulinemia. Finish with the practical lung-maturity tests and their thresholds. Focus for this checkpoint: Maternal diabetes complications, Hypoglycemia.

units.title: Pedersen hypothesis & Fetal diabetes complications
units.guide: Trace maternal hyperglycemia through infection, fluid, placental, and eye complications, then map the fetal and neonatal effects of fetal hyperinsulinemia. Finish with the practical lung-maturity tests and their thresholds. Focus for this checkpoint: Pedersen hypothesis, Fetal diabetes complications.

units.title: Neonatal diabetes complications → Lung maturity testing
units.guide: Trace maternal hyperglycemia through infection, fluid, placental, and eye complications, then map the fetal and neonatal effects of fetal hyperinsulinemia. Finish with the practical lung-maturity tests and their thresholds. Focus for this checkpoint: Neonatal diabetes complications, Late child outcomes, Lung maturity testing.

units.title: Lung maturity testing
units.guide: Trace maternal hyperglycemia through infection, fluid, placental, and eye complications, then map the fetal and neonatal effects of fetal hyperinsulinemia. Finish with the practical lung-maturity tests and their thresholds. Focus for this checkpoint: Lung maturity testing.

units.title: Shoulder dystocia → McRoberts maneuver
units.guide: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency with a recognizable turtle sign. Memorize the HELPERR-style escalation, the mechanics of McRoberts and internal rotations, prohibited fundal pressure, and maternal-fetal complications. Focus for this checkpoint: Shoulder dystocia, Shoulder dystocia management, McRoberts maneuver.

units.title: Shoulder dystocia management & Internal rotation
units.guide: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency with a recognizable turtle sign. Memorize the HELPERR-style escalation, the mechanics of McRoberts and internal rotations, prohibited fundal pressure, and maternal-fetal complications. Focus for this checkpoint: Shoulder dystocia management, Internal rotation.

units.title: Shoulder dystocia complications
units.guide: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency with a recognizable turtle sign. Memorize the HELPERR-style escalation, the mechanics of McRoberts and internal rotations, prohibited fundal pressure, and maternal-fetal complications. Focus for this checkpoint: Shoulder dystocia complications.

questions.q: How does the size of the thyroid gland normally change during pregnancy according to the notes?
opts: It remains unchanged and goitre is expected
It doubles only in the third trimester
It increases; a goitre remains pathological
It decreases and goitre is physiological
questions.exp: The thyroid gland increases in size in pregnancy, but goitre is still pathological. (Book p375)

questions.q: Which thyroid profile is described as normal in pregnancy?
opts: Overt hyperthyroid state with high free T4
Hypothyroid state with low total T4
Absent TSH secretion with low free hormones
Euthyroid state with normal free T3 and free T4
questions.exp: Pregnancy is a euthyroid state; free T3 and free T4 remain normal. (Book p375)

questions.q: Why do total T3 and total T4 rise in pregnancy?
opts: The fetal thyroid produces maternal T4
questions.exp: Estrogen raises TBG, increasing the protein-bound and therefore total T3/T4 values. (Book p375)

questions.q: What is the recommended daily iodine intake stated for pregnancy?
questions.exp: The stated RDA of iodine in pregnancy is 250 micrograms daily. (Book p375)

questions.q: Before 12 weeks of gestation, fetal development depends chiefly on:
opts: Maternal thyroxine because the fetal thyroid is not producing thyroxine
Fetal TSH crossing to the mother
questions.exp: Before 12 weeks, fetal thyroid thyroxine production is absent, so development depends on maternal thyroxine. (Book p375)

questions.q: At what point does fetal thyroid thyroxine production become present in the source notes?
opts: At or after 12 weeks of gestation
questions.exp: The fetal thyroid begins thyroxine production at or after 12 weeks. (Book p375)

questions.q: What is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in pregnancy in these notes?
questions.exp: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is listed as the most common cause of hypothyroidism. (Book p375)

questions.q: Which maternal thyroid-related substance cannot cross the placenta?
questions.exp: Maternal T3/T4 can cross the placenta, whereas maternal TSH cannot. (Book p375)

questions.q: When a woman treated for hypothyroidism conceives, by what range should her thyroxine dose be increased according to the notes?
questions.exp: The notes advise increasing thyroxine by 30–50% after conception in hypothyroidism. (Book p375)

questions.q: Fill up: In pregnancy total T4 rises because oestrogen increases ______, so the best screening test of thyroid function is ______.
questions.exp: Oestrogen raises TBG and hence total T4, which is why free T4 and TSH rather than total T4 are used to judge thyroid status in pregnancy. (Book p375)

questions.q: What is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism in pregnancy?
questions.exp: Graves' disease is identified as the most common cause of hyperthyroidism. (Book p375)

questions.q: Which antithyroid drug is preferred in the first trimester?
questions.exp: PTU is the drug of choice in the first trimester. (Book p375)

questions.q: Why are methimazole and carbimazole avoided in the first trimester?
opts: They prevent fetal thyroid formation after 20 weeks
They are associated with aplasia cutis and choanal atresia
questions.exp: Methimazole/carbimazole are avoided in T1 because of aplasia cutis and choanal atresia risk. (Book p375)

questions.q: Which option is contraindicated for hyperthyroidism during pregnancy?
questions.exp: Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in pregnancy. (Book p375)

questions.q: In thyroid storm during pregnancy, what is the drug of choice and what is used for symptomatic control?
questions.exp: The source lists PTU as the drug of choice for thyroid storm and propranolol for symptoms. (Book p375)

questions.q: A 28-year-old at 12 weeks with known Graves disease presents with fever of 39 C, a pulse of 150/min, profuse vomiting and new atrial fibrillation. What is the diagnosis and the first drug?
opts: Thyroid storm — start propylthiouracil, then iodine an hour later, with a beta blocker
Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis — reassure and repeat the thyroid profile in 4 weeks
Graves disease in pregnancy — start methimazole and plan radioiodine ablation after delivery now
Thyroid storm — start carbimazole and proceed to immediate delivery of the fetus
questions.exp: Thyroid storm is a medical emergency: propylthiouracil blocks both synthesis and T4-to-T3 conversion, iodine is given after an hour, and beta blockade controls the rate. (Book p375)

questions.q: Which placental hormone is prominently associated with insulin resistance in pregnancy?
questions.exp: hPL is listed among the hormones associated with insulin resistance in pregnancy. (Book p376)

questions.q: Which hormone is specifically noted as NOT producing insulin resistance in pregnancy?
questions.exp: The source distinguishes hCG as not causing insulin resistance. (Book p376)

questions.q: Significant insulin resistance in pregnancy typically develops around which gestational interval?
questions.exp: Significant insulin resistance develops around 24–28 weeks. (Book p376)

questions.q: Why is pregnancy described as a diabetogenic state?
opts: Progressing gestation increases hPL secretion and insulin resistance
Maternal insulin freely crosses to the fetus
questions.exp: Increasing hPL with gestation increases insulin resistance, making pregnancy diabetogenic. (Book p376)

questions.q: Which pairing of placental transfer is correct?
opts: Maternal insulin crosses; maternal glucose does not
Neither maternal glucose nor insulin crosses
Both cross equally by active transport
Maternal glucose crosses; maternal insulin does not
questions.exp: Maternal glucose crosses the placenta, whereas maternal insulin does not. (Book p376)

questions.q: A fetus is dependent on the mother primarily for which metabolic requirement?
questions.exp: The fetus depends on maternal glucose for its glucose requirement. (Book p376)

questions.q: Which urinary finding is stated to be normal in pregnancy?
questions.exp: Glycosuria is described as normal in pregnancy. (Book p376)

questions.q: Why should a pregnant woman with diabetes avoid fasting, vomiting, or diarrhea?
opts: They prevent glucose transfer to the fetus
They make maternal insulin cross the placenta
They can cause hypoglycemia followed by ketone-body formation and ketosis
questions.exp: Fasting, vomiting, or diarrhea can produce hypoglycemia, acetone bodies, and ketosis. (Book p376)

questions.q: Maternal hyperglycemia is considered fetotoxic chiefly because it promotes:
opts: Maternal insulin transfer to the fetus
Free-radical formation that crosses the placenta
questions.exp: Hyperglycemia increases free radicals that cross the placenta and contribute to congenital malformations. (Book p376)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about placental transfer in diabetic pregnancy is TRUE?
opts: Glucose crosses the placenta by facilitated diffusion but insulin does not, so the fetal pancreas makes its own insulin
Maternal insulin crosses the placenta freely and is the main driver of fetal macrosomia
Neither glucose nor insulin crosses the placenta, so the fetus depends on amino acids and lactate alone
Anti-TSH receptor antibodies cross the placenta, but neither glucose nor insulin can cross it
questions.exp: Maternal hyperglycaemia drives fetal hyperinsulinaemia because glucose crosses freely while insulin, and most oral agents such as glyburide, cross poorly. (Book p376)

questions.q: Which description best fits pregestational diabetes?
opts: A normoglycemic woman develops diabetes only after 24 weeks
It resolves within 6 weeks after delivery
It has no free-radical formation before organogenesis
A diabetic woman conceives and hyperglycemia is present from day 1
questions.exp: In pregestational diabetes, the woman is diabetic at conception and blood sugar is high from day 1. (Book p377)

questions.q: Why are congenital malformations characteristic of pregestational diabetes but not typical gestational diabetes?
opts: In GDM, free radicals form after organogenesis
Pregestational diabetes never produces free radicals
questions.exp: GDM usually develops later, with free radicals forming after organogenesis, so congenital malformations are not typical. (Book p377)

questions.q: What is the usual postpartum course of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM)?
opts: It resolves only after insulin therapy
It resolves within 6 weeks after delivery
It progresses immediately to type 1 diabetes
questions.exp: The notes state that GDM resolves within 6 weeks postpartum. (Book p377)

questions.q: In Priscilla White classification, type A diabetes in pregnancy refers to:
questions.exp: Type A in the Priscilla White classification denotes gestational diabetes. (Book p377)

questions.q: What differentiates A1 from A2 gestational diabetes?
opts: A1 is pregestational; A2 is gestational
A1 needs cesarean delivery; A2 never does
A1 has fetal echo; A2 has no ultrasound
A1 is diet controlled; A2 is controlled with insulin or metformin
questions.exp: A1 GDM is diet controlled, while A2 is controlled with medication such as insulin or metformin. (Book p377)

questions.q: GDM usually develops at what gestational age?
questions.exp: GDM usually develops between 24 and 28 weeks. (Book p377)

questions.q: GDM diagnosed before 20 weeks should generally raise suspicion for:
questions.exp: Diabetes diagnosed before 20 weeks is usually pregestational diabetes. (Book p377)

questions.q: Fill up: Universal screening for gestational diabetes is performed at ______ weeks, and women with strong risk factors are additionally tested ______.
questions.exp: All women are screened at 24-28 weeks, and those with risk factors are screened early at booking and retested later if the first test is normal. (Book p377)

questions.q: Which test timing is used to confirm the status of diabetes after GDM?
opts: A glucose test at 6 weeks postpartum
HbA1c on the day of delivery only
questions.exp: The source directs confirmation with a sugar-level test 6 weeks postpartum. (Book p377)

questions.q: For whom and when is TIFFA recommended in diabetes in pregnancy?
opts: Only women with fetal macrosomia in labor
All GDM and pregestational diabetes pregnancies at 18–20 weeks
questions.exp: TIFFA is done for both GDM and pregestational diabetes at 18–20 weeks. (Book p377)

questions.q: At a 2-hour postprandial glucose level of 200 mg/dL or more, what management is recommended irrespective of GDM versus pre-GDM?
opts: Repeat the test after six weeks
questions.exp: A 2-hour PP value of at least 200 mg/dL warrants 8 units of insulin regardless of diabetes category. (Book p377)

questions.q: All of the following are part of postpartum follow-up after gestational diabetes EXCEPT:
opts: Discharging her from follow-up once a single normal test is obtained at six weeks
A 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 6-12 weeks postpartum
Lifelong screening for diabetes every one to three years
Contraception and preconception counselling before the next pregnancy
questions.exp: Gestational diabetes marks a lifelong risk of type 2 diabetes, so surveillance every 1-3 years continues after the 6-12 week test. (Book p377)

questions.q: Which fasting blood sugar value meets the listed criterion for pregestational diabetes?
questions.exp: A fasting blood sugar of 126 mg/dL or greater meets the listed criterion. (Book p378)

questions.q: Which 2-hour postprandial blood sugar level meets the listed criterion for pregestational diabetes?
questions.exp: A 2-hour PPBS of 200 mg/dL or above meets the stated criterion. (Book p378)

questions.q: Which random blood sugar value is a clinical criterion for pregestational diabetes in the notes?
questions.exp: A random blood sugar of 200 mg/dL or greater is one of the clinical criteria. (Book p378)

questions.q: Which HbA1c threshold is used as a criterion for pregestational diabetes?
questions.exp: HbA1c of at least 6.5% is a listed criterion for pregestational diabetes. (Book p378)

questions.q: An HbA1c below 6.5% is associated with what gross congenital anomaly (GCA) risk in the notes?
questions.exp: The stated HbA1c band below 6.5% carries no GCA risk. (Book p378)

questions.q: What GCA risk is given for an HbA1c of 10% or higher?
questions.exp: The notes assign a 15–20% GCA risk to HbA1c of at least 10%. (Book p378)

questions.q: What HbA1c goal is stated for therapy in pregestational diabetes?
questions.exp: The stated therapeutic goal is HbA1c below 6%. (Book p378)

questions.q: Match the timing of poor diabetic control with its fetal consequence — 1) Periconception with HbA1c above 10% 2) Hyperglycaemia during organogenesis 3) Hyperglycaemia in the third trimester … A) Caudal regression, cardiac and renal anomalies B) Spontaneous abortion and major malformation C) Macrosomia, polyhydramnios and neonatal hypoglycaemia
questions.exp: Teratogenic damage happens in organogenesis and scales with HbA1c, whereas late hyperglycaemia drives fetal overgrowth and organomegaly. (Book p378)

questions.q: What is the diagnostic imaging tool for congenital anomalies in pregestational diabetes?
questions.exp: TIFFA is listed as the diagnostic tool for fetal congenital anomalies. (Book p378)

questions.q: Why is routine karyotyping not used for diabetic congenital-anomaly assessment?
opts: The concern is gross anomalies, whereas karyotyping detects chromosomal abnormalities
Karyotyping detects maternal diabetes and no other fetal condition
Karyotyping cannot technically be performed at all during pregnancy
Karyotyping is the definitive diagnostic test for a fetal VSD
questions.exp: Routine karyotyping is not used for diabetic congenital-anomaly assessment because the concern is gross congenital anomalies, whereas karyotyping detects chromosomal abnormalities. (Book p378)

questions.q: Which system is most commonly involved in congenital malformations of pregestational diabetes?
questions.exp: The cardiovascular system is the most commonly involved system, ahead of the CNS. (Book p378)

questions.q: What is the most common congenital malformation in pregestational diabetes?
questions.exp: VSD is listed as the most common congenital and cardiac malformation. (Book p378)

questions.q: Which cardiac anomaly is described as the most specific for maternal pregestational diabetes?
questions.exp: Transposition of the great arteries is the most specific cardiac anomaly in the notes. (Book p378)

questions.q: What is the most common cardiac finding in the fetus of a diabetic mother?
questions.exp: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy is listed as the most common cardiac finding. (Book p378)

questions.q: Which preconception measure is advised to reduce gross congenital anomalies in pregestational diabetes?
opts: Wait until fetal movements begin before acting
Switch to insulin before conception or once pregnancy is confirmed
Stop all glucose monitoring before conception
Start radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid
questions.exp: To reduce gross congenital anomalies in pregestational diabetes, switch to insulin before conception or once pregnancy is confirmed. (Book p378)

questions.q: What folic-acid schedule is listed for prevention of diabetic congenital anomalies?
opts: 400 micrograms daily started at 20 weeks and continued until delivery
No folic acid is advised, since diet alone supplies enough in diabetic pregnancy
400 micrograms daily from 1 month before conception to 3 months after
5 mg daily given only during labour and the immediate postpartum period
questions.exp: For prevention of diabetic congenital anomalies the listed schedule is 400 micrograms of folic acid daily, from 1 month before conception through 3 months after conception. (Book p378)

questions.q: Fill up: Women with pregestational diabetes are advised ______ mg of folic acid daily, because their pregnancies carry a higher risk of ______.
questions.exp: High-dose folic acid (4-5 mg) preconceptionally reduces the excess of neural tube defects seen in diabetic embryopathy. (Book p378)

questions.q: Which is a listed increased-risk complication in pregestational diabetes?
questions.exp: Pre-GDM is associated with increased risk of PIH. (Book p379)

questions.q: Which infection is specifically highlighted as an increased risk in pregestational diabetes?
questions.exp: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is specifically listed among increased infection risks. (Book p379)

questions.q: What happens to insulin resistance in pregestational diabetes across pregnancy?
opts: It disappears after the first trimester
It falls below normal in the third trimester
questions.exp: The notes list increased insulin resistance throughout pregnancy. (Book p379)

questions.q: At every antenatal visit in pregestational diabetes, which urinary screening is performed?
questions.exp: Each antenatal visit includes urine dipstick screening for proteinuria. (Book p379)

questions.q: How often is blood glucose monitored in the second trimester for pregestational diabetes?
questions.exp: Second-trimester blood-glucose monitoring is every 2 weeks. (Book p379)

questions.q: How often is blood glucose monitored in the third trimester for pregestational diabetes?
questions.exp: Third-trimester glucose monitoring is weekly. (Book p379)

questions.q: Why is fundal examination included in pregestational-diabetes follow-up?
questions.exp: Fundal examination is used to rule out diabetic retinopathy. (Book p379)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about antenatal surveillance in pregestational diabetes is TRUE?
opts: Serial growth scans and antepartum testing from 32-34 weeks are standard when control is poor or vasculopathy is present
Fetal karyotyping is mandatory because maternal diabetes raises the risk of fetal trisomy 21
Amniocentesis for lung maturity is required before every diabetic delivery, whatever the gestation
Serum alpha-fetoprotein screening is unreliable in diabetes and must never be offered
questions.exp: Surveillance intensity matches disease severity; diabetes does not raise aneuploidy risk, and AFP screening is still offered for neural tube defects. (Book p379)

questions.q: At what gestational age is fetal echocardiography done in pregestational diabetes to rule out VSD?
questions.exp: Fetal echocardiography is done at 22–24 weeks to rule out VSD. (Book p379)

questions.q: How often are urine routine and microscopy performed in pregestational diabetes?
questions.exp: Urine routine and microscopy are done in every trimester to assess asymptomatic bacteriuria. (Book p379)

questions.q: When should fetal surveillance begin in pregestational diabetes?
questions.exp: Fetal monitoring begins from 32 weeks in the stated plan. (Book p379)

questions.q: What is the listed frequency of NST and biophysical score in pregestational diabetes after surveillance begins?
opts: NST weekly and BPS only at delivery
questions.exp: The source recommends weekly NST and weekly biophysical score. (Book p379)

questions.q: Which growth-scan schedule is listed for pregestational diabetes?
opts: Only at 20 and 22 completed weeks of gestation
At 28-30 and 34-36 weeks, with at least a 3-week gap
Only once, at 12 completed weeks of gestation
Daily scans from 32 completed weeks until delivery
questions.exp: The listed growth-scan schedule for pregestational diabetes is at 28-30 and 34-36 weeks, with at least a 3-week gap. (Book p379)

questions.q: When is umbilical-artery Doppler indicated in diabetes in pregnancy?
opts: With diabetic vasculopathy or development of PIH
In all diet-controlled GDM at 10 weeks
questions.exp: Umbilical-artery Doppler is indicated for diabetic vasculopathy or PIH. (Book p380)

questions.q: Which medication is included to prevent PIH in pregestational diabetes management?
questions.exp: Low-dose aspirin is included for PIH prevention. (Book p380)

questions.q: What is described as the drug of choice for treatment of diabetes in pregnancy?
questions.exp: Insulin is listed as the drug of choice for diabetes treatment in pregnancy. (Book p380)

questions.q: A 32-year-old with type 1 diabetes at 10 weeks records fasting glucose of 130 mg/dL and two-hour postprandial values of 190 mg/dL on a twice-daily premixed insulin. What is the next step?
opts: Change to a basal-bolus regimen of short-acting and intermediate insulin and titrate to targets
Stop insulin and switch to metformin, since injected insulin is teratogenic in the first trimester
Add bedtime glyburide and continue the present insulin doses unchanged
Take no action, because glycaemic targets only matter in the third trimester
questions.exp: Insulin is the drug of choice in pregestational diabetes; a basal-bolus regimen with titration to fasting and postprandial targets is needed. (Book p380)

questions.q: When is termination/induction planned for pregestational diabetes in the source plan?
questions.exp: The planned termination/induction timing is 39 weeks or later. (Book p380)

questions.q: What is the default mode of delivery stated for diabetes in pregnancy?
questions.exp: Vaginal delivery is the default mode in the notes. (Book p380)

questions.q: What estimated fetal weight is listed as an indication for cesarean delivery in diabetes?
questions.exp: A fetal weight of 4.5 kg or more is a stated cesarean indication. (Book p380)

questions.q: Fill up: In well-controlled gestational diabetes without complications, delivery is planned around ______ weeks, while poorly controlled diabetes with vasculopathy is delivered by ______ weeks.
questions.exp: Uncomplicated well-controlled gestational diabetes is delivered at term, but vasculopathy or poor control shifts delivery earlier after documenting lung maturity. (Book p380)

questions.q: What mechanism underlies gestational diabetes in a previously normoglycemic woman?
opts: Failure of maternal insulin to cross the placenta
questions.exp: GDM occurs because increased insulin resistance develops in a previously normoglycemic woman. (Book p381)

questions.q: Which complication is specifically absent in GDM compared with pregestational diabetes?
questions.exp: The notes state that GDM has similar complications except gross congenital anomalies. (Book p381)

questions.q: Which investigation is NOT done in GDM because there is no suspected CVS anomaly?
questions.exp: Fetal echocardiography is omitted in GDM because congenital cardiac-anomaly suspicion is absent. (Book p381)

questions.q: When is the first DIPSI test recommended?
questions.exp: DIPSI screening begins at the first antenatal visit. (Book p381)

questions.q: If the first DIPSI screen is done early, when should it be repeated?
opts: At 24–28 weeks, after at least a 4-week gap
questions.exp: The test is repeated at 24–28 weeks with a minimum 4-week interval. (Book p381)

questions.q: How many DIPSI tests are needed if the first antenatal visit occurs after 28 weeks?
questions.exp: Only one DIPSI test is needed if the first visit is after 28 weeks. (Book p381)

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the DIPSI procedure?
opts: It is universal, nonfasting screening irrespective of the previous meal
It requires an overnight fast in selected women only
It is performed only after a positive urine test
It is limited to women with obesity
questions.exp: DIPSI is a universal screening test performed without fasting, irrespective of prior meals. (Book p381)

questions.q: What glucose load is used in the DIPSI test?
opts: 75 g glucose in 300 mL water, consumed in 5–10 minutes
50 g glucose in 100 mL water over 1 hour
questions.exp: DIPSI uses 75 g glucose in 300 mL water, consumed in 5–10 minutes. (Book p381)

questions.q: How is the DIPSI result checked?
opts: A random HbA1c immediately after the drink
A 2-hour postprandial value using a plasma-calibrated glucometer
questions.exp: The protocol checks 2-hour PP glucose using a plasma-calibrated glucometer. (Book p381)

questions.q: If vomiting occurs within 30 minutes of the glucose drink, what should be done?
opts: Repeat the test on another day
questions.exp: Vomiting within 30 minutes requires repeat testing on another day. (Book p381)

questions.q: Fill up: The DIPSI test uses ______ g of glucose regardless of the fasting state, and gestational diabetes is diagnosed when the two-hour value is ______ mg/dL or higher.
questions.exp: DIPSI is a single-step non-fasting 75 g test with a single two-hour cut-off of 140 mg/dL, which is why it suits busy antenatal clinics. (Book p381)

questions.q: If vomiting occurs after 30 minutes of the glucose drink, what should be done?
opts: Repeat the test on another day
questions.exp: If vomiting occurs after 30 minutes, the source directs that the test be continued. (Book p381)

questions.q: At the first antenatal visit, a 2-hour PP value below 140 mg/dL requires what next step?
questions.exp: A value below 140 at the first visit is repeated at 24–28 weeks. (Book p382)

questions.q: At the first antenatal visit, a 2-hour PP value of 140 mg/dL or more indicates:
questions.exp: A 2-hour PP value of 140 mg/dL or above at the first visit indicates GDM. (Book p382)

questions.q: At the first antenatal visit, a 2-hour PP value of 200 mg/dL or more indicates:
questions.exp: A 2-hour PP value of 200 mg/dL or more at the first visit indicates pregestational diabetes. (Book p382)

questions.q: At 24–28 weeks, which 2-hour PP value defines GDM?
questions.exp: At 24–28 weeks, a 2-hour PP value of 140 mg/dL or more defines GDM. (Book p382)

questions.q: For a 2-hour PP level of 140–199 mg/dL in GDM, what is the initial step?
questions.exp: The initial treatment for 140–199 mg/dL is medical nutrition therapy for 2 weeks. (Book p382)

questions.q: For a 2-hour PP level of 200 mg/dL or more in GDM, what immediate treatment is given?
opts: Aspirin with strict dietary salt restriction
8 units insulin plus medical nutrition therapy and weight counseling
Only daily walking for two weeks and then a review
No treatment at all until 32 weeks of gestation
questions.exp: For a 2-hour postprandial level of 200 mg/dL or more in GDM, the immediate treatment is 8 units of insulin plus medical nutrition therapy and weight counseling. (Book p382)

questions.q: A 30-year-old at 28 weeks is diagnosed with gestational diabetes (DIPSI two-hour value 165 mg/dL). After two weeks of medical nutrition therapy her fasting glucose is 98 mg/dL and her two-hour postprandial value is 130 mg/dL. What is the next step?
opts: Start insulin, or metformin if she declines insulin, while continuing nutrition therapy and glucose monitoring
Deliver the baby now, because medical nutrition therapy has failed
Add an oral hypoglycaemic agent only if targets remain uncontrolled after 36 weeks
Reassure her, because both readings are at target and no treatment is needed
questions.exp: Persistent fasting values above 95 mg/dL or postprandial values above 120 mg/dL despite two weeks of nutrition therapy call for pharmacotherapy. (Book p382)

questions.q: Which fasting plasma glucose target is stated for GDM?
questions.exp: The fasting glucose target is below 95 mg/dL. (Book p382)

questions.q: Which pair correctly states postprandial targets in GDM?
opts: 1-hour PP below 120 mg/dL and 2-hour PP below 140 mg/dL
1-hour PP below 140 mg/dL and 2-hour PP below 120 mg/dL
questions.exp: The stated targets are 1-hour PP <140 and 2-hour PP <120 mg/dL. (Book p382)

questions.q: Which HbA1c target is included in the GDM metabolic goals?
questions.exp: The GDM metabolic target includes HbA1c below 6%. (Book p382)

questions.q: What average capillary glucose target is stated?
questions.exp: The notes specify average capillary glucose below 100 mg/dL. (Book p382)

questions.q: If GDM metabolic goals are met with MNT, what is advised?
opts: Continue MNT and walk 30 minutes daily
questions.exp: When targets are met, continue MNT and advise a 30-minute daily walk. (Book p382)

questions.q: If metabolic goals are not met after initial MNT, what is the preferred escalation listed?
questions.exp: The notes list metformin before insulin when MNT goals are not met. (Book p382)

questions.q: How frequently are 2-hour PP values checked once follow-up begins in GDM?
opts: Every 2 weeks in T2 and weekly in T3, at least monthly
questions.exp: Follow-up is every 2 weeks in T2, weekly in T3, with a minimum monthly check. (Book p382)

questions.q: According to the listed GOI guideline, which treatment is chosen when GDM is diagnosed before 20 weeks?
questions.exp: The stated GOI guidance uses insulin for diagnosis before 20 weeks. (Book p382)

questions.q: Fill up: The usual glycaemic targets in pregnancy are a fasting glucose below ______ mg/dL and a two-hour postprandial glucose below ______ mg/dL.
questions.exp: Typical targets are fasting below 95 mg/dL, one-hour postprandial below 140 mg/dL and two-hour postprandial below 120 mg/dL. (Book p382)

questions.q: What macronutrient distribution is recommended in the balanced GDM meal plan?
questions.exp: The balanced meal is 40% carbohydrate, 40% fat, and 20% protein. (Book p383)

questions.q: How is the GDM diet distributed through the day?
opts: One large meal and one snack
questions.exp: The source distributes the diet over three meals and three snacks. (Book p383)

questions.q: What baseline caloric addition is advised for pregnant women in the nutrition plan?
questions.exp: The plan adds 350 kcal per day to all pregnant women. (Book p383)

questions.q: How is caloric intake adjusted for a BMI below 18.5 in the source plan?
questions.exp: BMI below 18.5 calls for an extra 500 kcal/day. (Book p383)

questions.q: How is caloric intake adjusted for a BMI above 25 in the source plan?
questions.exp: BMI above 25 calls for subtracting 500 kcal/day in the stated plan. (Book p383)

questions.q: In which diabetes category is metformin used according to these notes?
questions.exp: Metformin is recommended only in GDM, not in pregestational diabetes. (Book p383)

questions.q: After what gestational age is metformin used for GDM in the source notes?
questions.exp: Metformin is used only after 20 weeks of pregnancy. (Book p383)

questions.q: What is the stated first-line oral drug for GDM?
questions.exp: Metformin is described as the first-line oral drug and is recommended by the Government of India. (Book p383)

questions.q: For which patient phenotype is metformin specifically preferred?
opts: A woman with severe renal failure
questions.exp: The source states metformin is preferred in obese women. (Book p383)

questions.q: What is the maximum daily metformin dose in the source plan before insulin is added?
questions.exp: Metformin can be increased from 500 mg/day up to 2 g/day; higher requirement calls for insulin. (Book p383)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about medical nutrition therapy in gestational diabetes is TRUE?
opts: Energy is spread over three small meals and two or three snacks, with about 40-50% coming from low-glycaemic carbohydrate
Severe restriction to 1200 kcal a day improves outcomes by preventing fetal macrosomia
Avoiding carbohydrate altogether is the quickest way to reach glycaemic targets
Weight loss of about 1 kg a week is recommended for every woman with gestational diabetes
questions.exp: Ketosis from severe calorie or carbohydrate restriction is harmful; modest energy intake with distributed low-glycaemic carbohydrate is the goal. (Book p383)

questions.q: What is the most dangerous adverse effect of metformin listed in the notes?
questions.exp: Gastrointestinal effects are common, but lactic acidosis is the most dangerous listed adverse effect. (Book p383)

questions.q: What daily glyburide range is listed for GDM?
questions.exp: Glyburide is listed at 2.5 mg/day up to 20 mg/day. (Book p383)

questions.q: Which neonatal adverse effect is associated with glyburide in the source notes?
questions.exp: Glyburide is associated with increased neonatal hypoglycemia risk. (Book p383)

questions.q: All of the following statements about metformin in gestational diabetes are true EXCEPT:
opts: It is contraindicated in pregnancy because it causes severe fetal hypoglycaemia
It crosses the placenta freely, so the fetus is exposed to it
It is an option for women who refuse or cannot use insulin
Long-term offspring follow-up is reassuring but data remain incomplete
questions.exp: Metformin crosses the placenta and is used where insulin is refused or impractical; neonatal hypoglycaemia is far commoner with glyburide than metformin. (Book p383)

questions.q: What insulin preparation is recommended to start in the source algorithm?
questions.exp: The algorithm starts human premix insulin 30:70. (Book p384)

questions.q: What does the 30:70 human premix represent in the notes?
questions.exp: The stated premix contains 30 short-acting and 70 intermediate insulin. (Book p384)

questions.q: At what temperature should insulin be stored according to the notes?
questions.exp: Insulin storage is listed as 4–8°C. (Book p384)

questions.q: How many times may the insulin syringe be reused in the source notes?
questions.exp: The notes state that the syringe is reused 14 times. (Book p384)

questions.q: How does insulin requirement change as pregnancy advances and during labor?
opts: It rises with advancing pregnancy and falls in labor
It falls throughout pregnancy and rises in labor
It does not change at all
questions.exp: Insulin requirement increases with advancing gestation and decreases in labor when the patient is NPO. (Book p384)

questions.q: How is the initial premix insulin administered?
opts: Subcutaneously 30 minutes before breakfast once daily
questions.exp: Start premix 30:70 as a subcutaneous injection 30 minutes before breakfast once daily. (Book p384)

questions.q: What initial insulin dose corresponds to a 2-hour PP value of 120–160 mg/dL?
questions.exp: A 2-hour PP level of 120–160 mg/dL receives 4 units. (Book p384)

questions.q: What initial insulin dose corresponds to a 2-hour PP value of 160–200 mg/dL?
questions.exp: A 2-hour PP level of 160–200 mg/dL receives 6 units. (Book p384)

questions.q: What initial insulin dose corresponds to a 2-hour PP value above 200 mg/dL?
questions.exp: A 2-hour PP value above 200 mg/dL receives 8 units. (Book p384)

questions.q: Fill up: The usual starting total daily insulin dose in pregnancy is about ______ units per kg body weight, of which roughly ______ is given as basal insulin.
questions.exp: Total daily insulin starts at 0.7-1.0 units/kg, split so that about half is basal and half covers meals, then titrated to self-monitored glucose. (Book p384)

questions.q: After initiating insulin, when are glucose levels first rechecked in this algorithm?
questions.exp: The algorithm checks levels on the third day. (Book p384)

questions.q: If fasting blood sugar remains above 95 mg/dL after initial insulin, what adjustment is made?
opts: Add 2 units of insulin before dinner
questions.exp: Fasting glucose above 95 mg/dL prompts 2 additional units before dinner. (Book p384)

questions.q: If 2-hour PP remains above 120 mg/dL after initial insulin, what adjustment is made?
questions.exp: A 2-hour PP above 120 mg/dL prompts 2 additional units before breakfast. (Book p384)

questions.q: When may well-controlled diet-treated GDM (A1) be delivered?
questions.exp: Well-controlled A1 GDM is delivered at 39 weeks or later. (Book p385)

questions.q: When may poorly controlled drug-treated GDM (A2) be delivered?
questions.exp: Not-well-controlled A2 GDM is planned for delivery at 37 weeks or later. (Book p385)

questions.q: What is done with the morning medication dose in mild GDM on medical management during labor?
questions.exp: In mild GDM on medication, the morning dose is skipped during labor. (Book p385)

questions.q: How often is blood sugar monitored during labor in diabetes?
questions.exp: The intrapartum plan uses 2-hourly glucose monitoring with a glucometer. (Book p385)

questions.q: What IV fluid rate is used during labor in the stated diabetes protocol?
opts: Dextrose at 500 mL/hour for every patient
questions.exp: The labor protocol gives IV normal saline at 100 mL/hour, with insulin according to glucose. (Book p385)

questions.q: What insulin is added to 500 mL normal saline when intrapartum blood sugar is 120–140 mg/dL?
questions.exp: For 120–140 mg/dL, 4 units are added to 500 mL normal saline. (Book p385)

questions.q: What insulin is added to 500 mL normal saline when intrapartum blood sugar is 140–180 mg/dL?
questions.exp: For 140–180 mg/dL, 6 units are added to 500 mL normal saline. (Book p385)

questions.q: A woman with insulin-treated gestational diabetes presents in early labour at 39 weeks with a capillary glucose of 88 mg/dL. What is the intrapartum plan?
opts: Stop subcutaneous insulin, run a variable-rate insulin and dextrose infusion targeting 70-110 mg/dL, and stop it after delivery
Continue her usual subcutaneous insulin doses unchanged throughout labour
Give no insulin during labour and check the glucose only after delivery
Stop insulin and infuse 5% dextrose alone, without any glucose monitoring
questions.exp: Labour needs a sliding-scale insulin-dextrose infusion to keep glucose between 70 and 110 mg/dL, and requirements fall sharply once the placenta is delivered. (Book p385)

questions.q: What insulin is added to 500 mL normal saline when intrapartum blood sugar is 180 mg/dL or more?
questions.exp: For blood sugar at or above 180 mg/dL, 8 units are added to 500 mL normal saline. (Book p385)

questions.q: What is started if intrapartum blood glucose is below 70 mg/dL?
questions.exp: Hypoglycemia below 70 mg/dL is managed with IV 5% dextrose. (Book p385)

questions.q: When is blood sugar checked after delivery in GDM?
questions.exp: For GDM, blood sugar is checked on day 3 postpartum. (Book p385)

questions.q: What follow-up test is advised 6 weeks after discharge for GDM?
questions.exp: The source advises a 75-g 2-hour OGTT at 6 weeks after discharge. (Book p385)

questions.q: What ongoing screening is advised if the 6-week postpartum OGTT is normal after GDM?
questions.exp: A normal postpartum OGTT is followed by annual 75-g OGTT because of future type 2 diabetes risk. (Book p385)

questions.q: What happens to insulin requirement immediately after delivery in pregestational diabetes?
opts: It remains fixed for six weeks
It is permanently stopped in all cases
questions.exp: Insulin requirement decreases postpartum in pregestational diabetes. (Book p385)

questions.q: What medication transition is listed from day 2 after delivery in pregestational diabetes?
opts: Start methotrexate to suppress the puerperal endometrium
Shift back to oral hypoglycemic agents if they are needed
Start radioactive iodine ablation of the maternal thyroid
Stop all diabetic care and monitoring after delivery
questions.exp: From day 2 after delivery in pregestational diabetes, the listed transition is back to oral hypoglycemic agents if needed. (Book p385)

questions.q: Fill up: After delivery, insulin requirements in pregestational diabetes ______, and the postpartum dose is usually about ______ of the late-pregnancy dose.
opts: stay the same; the full dose
questions.exp: Loss of the placental hormones that cause insulin resistance means requirements plummet after delivery, often to half or less of the antenatal dose. (Book p385)

questions.q: Which set of infections is listed as increased in diabetes in pregnancy?
opts: Neonatal sepsis occurring in the first week of life
Asymptomatic bacteriuria, candidiasis and puerperal sepsis
Rubella, measles and mumps acquired during pregnancy
Urinary tuberculosis affecting the renal tract only
questions.exp: Infections listed as increased in diabetes in pregnancy are asymptomatic bacteriuria, candidiasis and puerperal sepsis. (Book p386)

questions.q: Polyhydramnios in diabetes can predispose to which obstetric emergency?
questions.exp: Polyhydramnios is linked to PTL, PROM, cord prolapse, PPH, and subinvolution. (Book p386)

questions.q: Oligohydramnios in a diabetic pregnancy suggests which associated pathology?
questions.exp: Oligohydramnios is noted when diabetic vasculopathy or PIH is present. (Book p386)

questions.q: What is the stated mechanism for placentomegaly in diabetes?
opts: Swelling of chorionic villi due to hyperglycemia
questions.exp: Hyperglycemia causes chorionic-villus swelling, producing a big placenta. (Book p386)

questions.q: What two placental complications are associated with diabetic placentomegaly?
opts: Placenta accreta and vasa previa only
questions.exp: The notes associate placentomegaly with increased PIH and placenta previa risk. (Book p386)

questions.q: Which eye assessment is essential in all women with pregestational diabetes?
questions.exp: All women with pre-GDM should have a baseline fundus examination because retinopathy can worsen. (Book p386)

questions.q: What blood sugar threshold defines hypoglycemia in the diabetes notes?
questions.exp: Hypoglycemia is defined as blood sugar below 70 mg/dL. (Book p386)

questions.q: What immediate oral option is listed for hypoglycemia?
opts: Three teaspoons of glucose in 100 mL water
Three teaspoons of salt in 100 mL water
questions.exp: The listed treatment is 3 teaspoons glucose in 100 mL water, or 6 teaspoons sugar in 100 mL water. (Book p386)

questions.q: All of the following are maternal complications of diabetes in pregnancy EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Pre-eclampsia, candidiasis, polyhydramnios, infections and progression of retinopathy and nephropathy are all linked to diabetes; placenta previa is not. (Book p386)

questions.q: In Pedersen hypothesis, maternal hyperglycemia first produces which fetal change?
questions.exp: Maternal hyperglycemia causes fetal hyperglycemia before stimulating the fetal pancreas. (Book p387)

questions.q: What endocrine state results after fetal hyperglycemia stimulates the fetal pancreas?
questions.exp: Fetal hyperglycemia stimulates the fetal pancreas, producing hyperinsulinemia. (Book p387)

questions.q: How does fetal hyperinsulinemia contribute to shoulder dystocia?
opts: It increases growth and fat deposition around the fetal shoulder
questions.exp: Fetal hyperinsulinemia promotes macrosomia and shoulder fat deposition, leading to shoulder dystocia. (Book p387)

questions.q: IUGR in a diabetic pregnancy is expected primarily when which condition coexists?
questions.exp: The notes restrict IUGR in diabetes to cases with vasculopathy or PIH. (Book p387)

questions.q: Which hormones are identified as needed for fetal growth?
questions.exp: Insulin and IGFs are named as hormones needed for fetal growth. (Book p387)

questions.q: Uncontrolled diabetes raises the risk of which early pregnancy outcome?
questions.exp: Uncontrolled diabetes increases the risk of abortion. (Book p387)

questions.q: Why is stillbirth risk increased in diabetes according to the source?
opts: All diabetic fetuses have structural renal anomalies
Macrosomia raises oxygen demand and hyperglycemia causes oxidative stress and chorionic-villus edema
Maternal insulin crosses and causes fetal bradycardia
questions.exp: Macrosomia increases oxygen demand, while hyperglycemia causes oxidative stress and villous edema that reduce oxygen transport. (Book p387)

questions.q: When is diabetic stillbirth most common according to the notes?
opts: In the last 2 weeks of pregnancy
questions.exp: The notes state that diabetic stillbirth is most common in the last 2 weeks of pregnancy. (Book p387)

questions.q: Match the mechanism with its consequence — 1) Pedersen hypothesis 2) Diabetic embryopathy in the first trimester 3) Neonatal hypoglycaemia after cord clamping … A) Caudal regression and cardiac anomalies B) Fetal hyperinsulinaemia causing macrosomia and organomegaly C) Continued fetal insulin action once the maternal glucose supply stops
questions.exp: Maternal hyperglycaemia drives fetal hyperinsulinaemia (Pedersen), early hyperglycaemia malforms the embryo, and sustained fetal insulin causes postnatal hypoglycaemia. (Book p387)

questions.q: Why does neonatal hypoglycemia occur after a diabetic pregnancy?
opts: Maternal glucose supply stops at birth while fetal insulin remains high
Maternal insulin starts crossing after birth
Fetal insulin production stops abruptly before birth
The placenta continues supplying glucose after birth
questions.exp: At birth maternal glucose supply is lost but fetal insulin remains high, causing neonatal hypoglycemia. (Book p387)

questions.q: Which neonatal electrolyte abnormalities are listed as triggered by hypoglycemia?
questions.exp: Hypocalcemia, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia are listed with neonatal hypoglycemia. (Book p387)

questions.q: Why is respiratory distress syndrome increased in the infant of a diabetic mother?
opts: Maternal glucose cannot cross the placenta
It is caused only by fetal anemia
questions.exp: High fetal insulin suppresses surfactant production, increasing RDS risk. (Book p387)

questions.q: Hypoxia in the infant of a diabetic mother leads to which sequence?
opts: Increased erythropoietin, polycythemia, hyperviscosity, and hyperbilirubinemia
questions.exp: Hypoxia raises erythropoietin, causing polycythemia, hyperviscosity, and hyperbilirubinemia. (Book p387)

questions.q: Which complication is specifically NOT seen in the neonatal complication list of diabetes?
questions.exp: The source explicitly notes that anemia is not seen as a neonatal complication. (Book p387)

questions.q: Which late outcome is listed for a child born after a diabetic pregnancy?
questions.exp: Late child outcomes include obesity, metabolic syndrome, and a 1–3% risk of type 2 diabetes. (Book p388)

questions.q: How is fetal lung maturity testing performed according to the notes?
opts: By amniocentesis in the third trimester
By fetal echocardiography in the first trimester
questions.exp: Lung maturity tests are done on amniotic fluid obtained by third-trimester amniocentesis. (Book p388)

questions.q: What is the most common fetal lung-maturity test listed?
questions.exp: The lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio is listed as the most common lung-maturity test. (Book p388)

questions.q: What L/S ratio indicates mature fetal lungs in the notes?
questions.exp: An L/S ratio of 2:1 or greater indicates lung maturity. (Book p388)

questions.q: Which is identified as the best lung-maturity test when done at or after 35 weeks?
questions.exp: Phosphatidylglycerol is the best test, done at or after 35 weeks. (Book p388)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the infant of a diabetic mother is TRUE?
opts: Fetal hyperinsulinaemia antagonises cortisol and delays surfactant maturation, raising the risk of respiratory distress at any gestation
Neonatal hypoglycaemia is rare, because the fetal pancreas involutes promptly after delivery
Neonatal polycythaemia and jaundice result from fetal hypo-insulinaemia and reduced oxygen consumption
Amniocentesis to document lung maturity is mandatory before every delivery in a diabetic pregnancy
questions.exp: Hyperinsulinaemia delays surfactant, chronic intrauterine hyperglycaemia drives polycythaemia, and lung maturity testing is selective, not universal. (Book p388)

questions.q: What does the presence of phosphatidylglycerol indicate?
questions.exp: Presence of phosphatidylglycerol indicates lung maturity. (Book p388)

questions.q: Which lamellar-body count guarantees 100% lung maturity in the notes?
questions.exp: A lamellar-body count above 50,000/mL indicates 100% mature lungs. (Book p388)

questions.q: What lamellar-body count is considered a positive test in amniotic fluid?
questions.exp: A lamellar-body count of 30,000–40,000/mL AF is termed positive. (Book p388)

questions.q: In the obsolete Nile blue sulfate test, what result indicates mature lungs?
questions.exp: Orange cells are mature skin cells; more than 50% orange cells indicates mature lungs. (Book p388)

questions.q: Fill up: Phosphatidylglycerol appears in amniotic fluid at about ______ weeks, and its presence is taken to indicate ______.
questions.exp: A lecithin-sphingomyelin ratio of 2:1 and the appearance of phosphatidylglycerol around 35 weeks both indicate that the fetal lungs are mature. (Book p388)

questions.q: How is shoulder dystocia defined in the source notes?
opts: Inability to deliver the fetal shoulder within 1 minute of head delivery
Failure to deliver the head within 10 minutes of crowning
Any prolonged second stage over 2 hours
questions.exp: Shoulder dystocia is inability to deliver the fetal shoulder within 1 minute after head delivery. (Book p388)

questions.q: What is the turtle sign in shoulder dystocia?
opts: Recession of the fetal head into the perineum
questions.exp: The turtle sign is recession of the delivered fetal head back into the perineum. (Book p388)

questions.q: Fill up: The first manoeuvre for shoulder dystocia is ______, which works by ______.
opts: McRoberts positioning; flattening the lumbar lordosis and rotating the symphysis pubis upwards
fundal pressure; driving the anterior shoulder below the symphysis pubis
the Zavanelli manoeuvre; replacing the head before caesarean delivery
the Woods corkscrew; widening the bisacromial diameter of the shoulders
questions.exp: Hyperflexing the maternal thighs on the abdomen flattens the sacral promontory and rotates the symphysis, freeing the impacted anterior shoulder. (Book p388)

questions.q: What is the first action in the listed shoulder-dystocia management sequence?
opts: Proceed directly to cesarean before assessment
questions.exp: The sequence begins by calling for help. (Book p389)

questions.q: Which early surgical adjunct is listed in shoulder-dystocia management?
questions.exp: The management sequence includes liberal episiotomy. (Book p389)

questions.q: What is the first and most effective maneuver for shoulder dystocia?
questions.exp: McRoberts maneuver is described as the first and most effective maneuver. (Book p389)

questions.q: What does the McRoberts maneuver involve?
opts: Delivery of the posterior arm first
Flexion and abduction of the legs against the abdomen
Extension of both legs below the table
Internal rotation of one shoulder only
questions.exp: McRoberts uses flexion and abduction of the maternal legs against the abdomen. (Book p389)

questions.q: Why does the McRoberts maneuver help shoulder dystocia?
opts: It rotates both fetal shoulders internally at the pelvic brim
It decreases the bisacromial diameter of the fetal shoulders
It straightens the sacrum and increases the space available
It increases the bony pelvic diameter by about 5 cm
questions.exp: The McRoberts manoeuvre straightens the sacrum relative to the lumbar spine and increases the available space, without increasing the pelvic diameter. (Book p389)

questions.q: What is added if McRoberts maneuver alone fails?
questions.exp: If McRoberts fails, sustained suprapubic pressure in thrusts is added. (Book p389)

questions.q: Which maneuver performs manual rotation of the shoulders in shoulder dystocia?
questions.exp: The Enter maneuver is manual rotation of the shoulders. (Book p389)

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares Wood's corkscrew and Rubin maneuvers?
opts: Wood's corkscrew rotates both shoulders; Rubin rotates one shoulder
Wood's rotates one shoulder; Rubin rotates both
questions.exp: Wood's corkscrew acts on both shoulders, whereas Rubin's maneuver acts on one. (Book p389)

questions.q: What is the maneuver called when the posterior fetal arm is delivered?
questions.exp: Delivery of the posterior arm is the Jacquemier maneuver. (Book p389)

questions.q: Which maneuver places the mother on all fours?
questions.exp: The all-fours maneuver is Gaskin maneuver. (Book p389)

questions.q: What is the last-step Zavanelli maneuver?
opts: Push the fetal head back into the uterus and perform cesarean section
Deliver the posterior arm with traction
questions.exp: Zavanelli replaces the fetal head into the uterus before cesarean delivery. (Book p389)

questions.q: What can be done for shoulder dystocia in a dead baby according to the notes?
questions.exp: For a dead baby, clavicular fracture (cleidotomy) is listed. (Book p389)

questions.q: Which intervention is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia management?
questions.exp: Fundal pressure is specifically contraindicated. (Book p389)

questions.q: What is the maximum time allowed for each shoulder-dystocia maneuver before moving to the next step?
questions.exp: Each maneuver is performed for a maximum of 30 seconds before escalating. (Book p389)

questions.q: McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure have failed and the anterior shoulder is still impacted behind the symphysis. Which manoeuvre should be attempted next?
opts: Internal rotation with Woods corkscrew or Rubin II, or delivery of the posterior arm
Fundal pressure applied by an assistant while traction continues
Immediate Zavanelli manoeuvre and caesarean delivery
Symphysiotomy before any rotational manoeuvre is attempted
questions.exp: After McRoberts and suprapubic pressure, internal rotation or posterior arm delivery reduces the bisacromial diameter; fundal pressure is contraindicated. (Book p389)

questions.q: What is the most common fetal complication of shoulder dystocia?
questions.exp: Erb's palsy is listed as the most common fetal complication. (Book p389)

questions.q: What arm position is characteristic of Erb palsy (policeman/porter tip hand)?
opts: Both arms held above the head
Flexed at elbow with hyperextended wrist only
questions.exp: The source describes Erb palsy as an internally rotated, adducted, and pronated arm. (Book p389)

questions.q: What is the most common maternal complication of shoulder dystocia?
questions.exp: Postpartum hemorrhage is the most common maternal complication. (Book p389)

questions.q: Which nerve is most commonly injured during McRoberts maneuver?
opts: The facial nerve, compressed against the maternal symphysis pubis
The ulnar nerve, compressed at the elbow during positioning
The phrenic nerve, stretched by the hyperflexed thighs
The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, compressed under the inguinal ligament
questions.exp: Hyperflexing the thighs compresses the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh under the inguinal ligament, causing meralgia paraesthetica. (Book p389)

questions.q: All of the following are recognised fetal complications of shoulder dystocia EXCEPT:
opts: Fracture of the clavicle or humerus
questions.exp: Brachial plexus injury, long-bone fracture and asphyxia follow traumatic delivery and prolonged head-to-body interval; talipes is not caused by shoulder dystocia. (Book p389)
